explore.adds_to_baseline: Essentially nothing measurable on top of colour. Fusion: gradients at weight 0.2 are numerically inert (every number identical to the baseline: block 0.953, start 0.967, contact 0.954, A-vs-B 0.954, B-vs-R(c2) 0.955). At weight 0.5 they only add noise (block 0.937, clip2 0.916, contact 0.917, B-vs-R(c2) 0.919, all below baseline). The class-mean chi2 gap is about 0.005-0.05 for the gradient histograms versus about 0.5-0.7 for HSV, so gradients cannot move the decision except as noise. As a colour-free cue, they do separate the smooth, upright referee suit from a creased gi: B-vs-R on clip2 is 0.82-0.87 for HOG (nn and mean), edge-density, structure-tensor and orientation-histogram variants, with no colour or darkness threshold. That is still below the HSV histogram's 0.955, which already handles that pair, so there is nothing for it to rescue. The navy-suit failure is in the colour thresholds, not in the histogram. Gradient-only A-vs-B tops out at 0.723 (hog_body_log_nn), and under contact at 0.680 versus 0.954 for colour.
explore.failure_modes: (1) Spatial HOG is dominated by pose and by which body overlaps which. With class-mean prototypes it sits at chance on clip1 block (0.348 for gray, 0.349 for log-grey, against a chance level of 0.333) and below chance on the start protocol (clip1 start 0.128-0.141). Exemplar matching helps (hog_body_log_nn: block 0.664, contact 0.680) but still fails the start protocol (clip1 0.316). The torso/legs split and 32px cells were worse. (2) Gradient statistics mostly encode capture conditions, not identity: sharpness and motion blur, compression, exposure (the white gi is over-exposed, so its folds have little contrast), and crop scale. That makes the clip1 numbers unstable. multiscale_energy_nn is best on clip1 block (0.811) but collapses on the held-out clip2 (block 0.528, start 0.372), under contact (0.461 block, 0.361 start) and on B-vs-R(c2) (0.640), and in the start protocol it is only 0.534 overall. Its clip1 result is clip-specific and should not be trusted. (3) The person mask is a union of all people in the frame, so in contact the crop pools both bodies' gradients and the markers cannot say whose texture it is. (4) The best pure-gradient variant by clip2 or contact accuracy would be hog_body_log_nn or edge_density_grid, but those were not chosen, because selection was by clip1 only. Even so, no gradient variant exceeds 0.68 on clip2 or contact (baseline 0.940 and 0.954). (5) The gradient variants differ from the baseline in that A-vs-B is nearly colour-free, and A-vs-B and contact are the two hardest cases for them (0.47-0.72).
explore.notes: Result: gradient and HOG markers do NOT beat the HSV torso baseline and should not replace or be added to it. The best pure-gradient variant by clip1 block is multiscale_energy_nn (clip1 0.811) but it generalises poorly to clip2 (0.528). Variants 12 and 15 are fusion diagnostics that include the colour baseline. They are not gradient markers, so they were excluded from best-selection. Strict clip1-block ranking would otherwise give the baseline-equivalent fusion (0.972), which says nothing about gradients. All 15 variants (the limit) are listed. Metric and mode were fixed a priori per feature type (cos for HOG, chi2 for L1 histograms, l2 for statistic vectors). Variants 13-15 were chosen after the round-1 clip1 numbers. 13 and 14 are the exemplar-mode counterparts of the best statistic variant and of HOG. 15 is the light fusion weight. clip2 was never used for any choice. Implementation notes: the harness cannot use cv2.HOGDescriptor because OpenCV 5.0.0.93 has no HOGDescriptor, and skimage is not installed. HOG is therefore a plain-numpy implementation (soft orientation binning, overlapping 2x2 block L2-Hys). It matches a naive loop reference to 8e-14. Only interior gradients are used (person mask eroded 3 px), so silhouette shape does not leak in. Zones are row fractions (head 0-.20, torso .20-.55, legs .55-1), not keypoints. Crops are resized to a canonical size for HOG so crop width and aspect cannot leak. No absolute position, frame number or crop size is used. No darkness threshold is used. Log-grey removes the dark-cloth/low-gradient confound. The baseline's own colour reference run matched the stated numbers (block 0.953, start 0.967). Timing: best variant about 1.4-1.7 ms per instance cold (all 324 instances, 3 repeats, no cache; the full gradient pipeline is 0.7-2.2 ms per instance across variants). Files: only tools/markers/gradient_hog.py was added by this task. tools/markers/colour_profile.py is untracked and belongs to another worker.

verify.leakage_detail:
No explicit leakage, but there is an implicit scale and context confound that inflates the clip1 number.

Explicit channels (none found). multiscale_energy reads only d["crop"] (BGR image and mask). The values are mask-weighted means per row-fraction zone, so mask area and crop width are normalised out. Box position, frame, label and clip appear only in the cache key _key(), not in the feature value. A random horizontal roll of crop and mask gives block 0.678 (c1 0.777, c2 0.586), essentially unchanged, so there is no dependence on horizontal position. The feature abstains on 0 of 324 instances.

Harness controls. Label shuffles all collapse to chance, 30 seeds each, nn protocol, block / start:
- within 24-frame blocks: 0.352 / 0.337 (A-vs-B 0.50)
- within frame: 0.362 / 0.336
- within clip: 0.341 / 0.352
So the block-level class mix and the frame identity are not exploitable.

Implicit leakage (found). The crop is resized to 192 px from boxes of very different heights, and clip1 R boxes are about 435 px against about 244 px (A) and 286 px (B). The band energy depends on that resize, so crop scale leaks in.
- Regressing each feature dim on log box height gives mean R^2 0.46 (clip1) and 0.37 (clip2). Within clip1 class A it is 0.56.
- Residualising the marker on log box height (quadratic, per clip) drops block from 0.662 to 0.577 and clip1 from 0.811 to 0.663. About 0.15 of the clip1 headline is scale.
- Within one class, the nearest neighbour in feature space recovers the time order well even with the plus or minus 1 block exclusion: Spearman rho 0.65 (clip1 A), 0.36 (clip2 A), 0.18 (clip2 B), 0.07 (clip1 B). Log box height alone gives 0.56 / 0.48 / 0.65 / 0.28.
- The same statistic computed on background-only pixels (outside the dilated mask) scores block 0.717 (c1 0.694, c2 0.725), higher than the person feature. Context in the crop is as class-informative as the body, so the 0.66 cannot be credited to body appearance. Filling the background with a constant before the DoG, or using normalised convolution, gives 0.676 and 0.640. So the marker itself does not read background gradients; its signal is person pixels plus scale and silhouette.
- Reference only, not used by the marker: absolute position (cx, cy) alone gives block 0.680, and log box height alone 0.467. A forbidden feature would match this marker.
- A random vertical roll drops block to 0.476, so the marker depends on the head/torso/legs layout, which is pose-like structure.
- The person mask is a union of all people. The montage shows both athletes inside one A outline, and clip2 referee crops containing athlete pixels, so contact crops pool bodies.

Per-class block confusion:
- clip1 no-contact: A 1.00, B 0.70, R 0.91.
- clip1 contact: A 0.55, B 0.71.
- clip2 contact: A 0.61, B 0.29, R 0.33.
Contact accuracy 0.461 with n=163, so near or below chance.
verify.reasoning:
Reproduced. I re-ran multiscale_energy_nn (l2, nn) through tools.marker_eval.evaluate from scratch and got exactly the explorer's numbers:
- block: bal 0.662, contact 0.461 (n=163), clip1 0.811, clip2 0.528, A-vs-B 0.688, B-vs-R(c2) 0.640
- start: bal 0.534, contact 0.361, clip1 0.733, clip2 0.372, A-vs-B 0.593, B-vs-R(c2) 0.498
- abstain 0
- baseline re-run: block 0.953, start 0.967

The explorer's stated 0.662 / 0.534 / 0.811 / 0.528 all match to 3 decimals. The explorer's file is also untracked in git, so I could not check edit order.

Cherry-picking check. I re-ran all 15 listed variants and every reported number (block, clip2_block, start, clip1_block) matches within 0.001. The count is 15, within the limit. Selection looks clip1-only: variant 13 has the best clip1 block among the pure-gradient variants (0.811; the fusion variants 12 and 15 score 0.972 but are labelled diagnostics). If the explorer had picked on clip2, edge_density_grid (clip2 0.677) or hog_body_log_nn (clip2 0.664, contact 0.680) would have been chosen instead, so the choice worked against clip2. Variants 13-15 were added after seeing round-1 output that printed both clips, which I cannot rule out as an influence, but nothing indicates clip2 steered them. The reported negative result is honest and reproducible.

Does a gradient marker add anything? No.
- Best of all 15 non-fusion variants: block 0.664 (hog_body_log_nn), against 0.953 for the baseline.
- Best contact: 0.680 (hog_body_log_nn), against 0.954.
- Fusion with HSV (chi2, mean): w=0.5 gives 0.937 block, below baseline; w=0.2 gives 0.953 / 0.940 / 0.967, identical to baseline. Gradients contribute no information on top of colour.

Why it fails, as confirmed here:
- The marker largely encodes crop scale and capture conditions: R^2 of 0.37-0.46 against log box height, and its time-order recovery within a class is comparable to log box height alone.
- Its clip1 headline of 0.811 falls to 0.663 once scale is regressed out.
- The same statistic on background pixels scores as well as or better than on the body (0.717).
- Only A-vs-B is partly usable, at about 0.69-0.72 and not robust to the start protocol. That is far below the baseline's 0.954.

Verdict: do_not_use for identifying a unique body, and in particular not for the navy-suit referee versus blue-gi athlete problem (B-vs-R clip2 0.64 / 0.50 against baseline 0.955 / 0.984). The explorer's conclusion that the gradient family does not beat the baseline is correct and its failure-mode description is supported by my tests.

Cost (best variant): about 1.35 ms per instance cold, feature only (4 Gaussian blurs on a 192xW crop). That is cheap but irrelevant given the accuracy.

explore.adds_to_baseline: The selected profile does not beat the baseline overall. What it adds is complementary errors. It makes 0 errors on clip1, where the baseline makes 6 (5 B->A, 1 B->R, nearly all on non-contact instances). It also fixes the baseline's 3 non-contact clip2 A errors. Its own 13 errors all sit on clip2 and 12 of 13 are contact instances. The baseline's errors are mostly non-contact (10/161 non-contact vs 5/163 contact). Only 5 instances are wrong for both (profile wrong and baseline right: 8; baseline wrong and profile right: 10). That pattern suggests a fusion could help, with the profile covering free-standing bodies and the baseline covering overlap. I did not test a fusion, and it is outside this family. A-vs-B is 0.969 vs 0.954, a gap of about 4 of 260 decisions, so it is within noise. The l1 sibling (not selected under the protocol) is the only variant that beat the baseline on block (0.981), contact (0.968), A-vs-B (0.973) and B-vs-R clip2 (0.981). Its start accuracy (0.936) stayed below the baseline (0.967), and its clip2 advantage cannot count as validated, because l1 was only distinguishable from l2 through held-out clip2.
explore.failure_modes: All 13 clip2 errors of the selected variant: B->A 8, R->B 4, A->R 1. 12 of the 13 are contact instances. Hypothesis, not tested: under overlap the person mask contains both bodies, so band medians are dominated by the white athlete and the blue athlete's profile drifts toward the white prototype. The same mixing probably produces the R->B errors, where the navy referee overlaps a blue gi. The baseline instead uses a torso patch from keypoints. The start protocol (gallery from the first 30%) is weaker, 0.927 vs baseline 0.967, and clip2 start is 0.867. The bands are equal slices of the box and are not anchored to body parts, so ground work (horizontal bodies) makes bands mean different things across poses. I did not try pose-anchored bands. The best variant uses Lab lightness L, so it uses darkness. This is not label leakage, because R was labelled by exclusion and not by colour. The brightness-free versions (ab and gradients, hue-vector, rg chromaticity) were all below the baseline and below the Lab variants (block 0.768-0.932, clip2 0.736-0.885). Brightness is therefore what separates the navy suit from the blue gi, and the gradient on its own does not recover it. The hue-vector and chromaticity profiles were far worse even on clip1 (0.899 and 0.869 vs 0.986 for a*b*). Likely cause, not verified: both are noisy for dark and low-saturation pixels. Protocol caveat: clip1 block is saturated (1.000 for three variants: l2, l1 and cos on the same features), so clip1 cannot rank them. The metric choice was settled by the tie rule (fewer dims, then clip1 start, then the l2 default), and that picked l2. l1 is 0.044 higher on clip2 block (0.957 vs 0.913), but that was never allowed to drive selection. A third clip is needed to settle l1 vs l2. Selection rule applied: highest clip1 block balanced accuracy.
explore.notes: I used 13 of the 15 allowed variants and left 2 unused. All 13 are listed in variants_tried, and the module's FEATURES dict holds exactly those 13, with the metric and mode for each in METRIC. Every harness call was appended to a log in the scratchpad, so the count is auditable. The staging was: colour space first, then band count, statistic and gradient on the clip1-leading Lab space, then mode, metric, K=12 with gradients, and a brightness-free gradient variant. Each stage was chosen from clip1 numbers. clip2 was only read as a report. The selection rule was set before the stage-3 results: highest clip1 block balanced accuracy, then fewer dimensions, then clip1 start, then the l2 default. Lab_K6_med_gradboth, Lab_K6_med_gradboth_l1 and Lab_K6_med_gradboth_cos all reach 1.000 on clip1 block. They tie on dimensions, and clip1 start (1.000, 0.990, 1.000) removes only l1, so the l2 default decided it. Lab_K12_med_gradboth (clip1 block 0.995, clip2 0.941, block 0.968) is a no-ranking-power caveat: it sits within 0.005 of 1.000 on clip1 but has more dimensions (67 vs 33). I did not pick it for its clip2 number. Feature recipe: the 192-px crop is split into K equal horizontal bands. Each band takes the median of Lab (L scaled x0.5, a*, b*) over person-mask pixels, with the mask eroded by 2 px and bands under 20 mask pixels filled by the whole-body median. Adjacent-band differences are appended, so K=6 gives 18 + 15 = 33 dimensions. No absolute position, frame number, crop width, or other segment-identifying information is used. No instance abstained (a mask under 200 px would). Timing is 3.1 ms per instance on average (median 1.8, p95 8.1), measured on CPU with the colour-conversion cache cleared per instance. The tools/markers/gradient_hog.py file in the working tree is not mine and I did not touch it. My only repo change is tools/markers/colour_profile.py. A runner is at python -m tools.markers.colour_profile [variant names], run with PYTHONPATH=. from the repo root.

verify.leakage_detail:
Code read (tools/markers/colour_profile.py): the feature is 33-D (6 band medians x (0.5*L,a,b) = 18, plus 15 adjacent-band differences) computed only from mask pixels of the 192-px-high crop. Bands are fractions of crop height. It does not use frame, clip, box position, crop width, or any absolute coordinate. Two implicit channels exist: the mask shapes which pixels enter the medians, and bands with fewer than 20 mask pixels are filled with the whole-body median. The mask is not a label source. I found no leakage in any of these tests (all run in the scratchpad, no repo files touched):
(1) Labels shuffled within (clip, 24-frame block), 5 seeds: block bal_acc 0.29-0.40 (chance 0.33). It collapses as it should.
(2) Crop randomisation fed to the feature. Horizontal roll gives 0.950 and horizontal flip gives 0.955, both unchanged as expected since bands are horizontal. Vertical scale/shift jitter gives 0.934. Scrambling pixel positions inside the mask gives 0.924. Row permutation gives 0.867. Random vertical roll gives 0.874. So the signal is mostly global colour (the pixel-shuffle control still scores 0.924), and the vertical profile and gradients add about 0.03 block and 0.07 on contact. Nothing in it is positional.
(3) Nuisance-only features with no colour. Crop aspect gives 0.546, mask fraction 0.353, band mask fractions 0.467, band mask widths 0.499, all geometry combined 0.542, and frame number alone 0.410 (clip2 0.333). Geometry carries some R-vs-athlete information (R crops are about 70 px wide vs about 145 px in clip1, and R never has contact in clip1), but the feature does not encode it and the result is far from 0.955.
(4) Same-frame pair assignment, where time, segment and lighting are identical for both bodies: clip1 AB 69/69, AR 22/22, BR 22/22. Clip2 AB 49/51 (0.961), AR 42/42, BR 42/42. The baseline scores AB 0.971 on clip1 and 1.000 on clip2.
(5) Leave-one-segment-out (also excluding frames within 24 of the test frame) gives 0.955 (clip1 1.000, clip2 0.913), the same as the block protocol.
(6) Cross-clip transfer (train on one clip, test on the other) gives 0.895 for clip1->clip2 and 0.963 for clip2->clip1. The baseline gets 0.874 and 0.930. The feature really transfers.
Caveats that are not leakage: the class and contact structure of the dataset makes some geometry weakly informative (see 3). Contact flags are 0% for R in clip1 vs about 42% for A/B.
verify.reasoning:
REPRODUCTION: I re-ran Lab_K6_med_gradboth (l2, mean) with the harness and got block 0.955 (clip1 1.000, clip2 0.913, contact 0.913, A-vs-B 0.969, B-vs-R(c2) 0.934) and start 0.927 (clip1 1.000, clip2 0.867, contact 0.903). These match the explorer exactly. I also re-ran all 13 registered variants, and every block, start and clip2 number matches the explorer's variants_tried list. The explorer's clip2 error breakdown reproduces too: 13 errors (B->A 8, R->B 4, A->R 1), 12 of them on contact instances.

PROTOCOL / CHERRY-PICKING: There are 13 variants (within the budget of 15) and the file lists all of them, including the bad ones. Clip1 block accuracies are: ab 0.986, Lab 0.996, K3 0.986, K12 0.996, mean-stat 0.970, K12 gradboth 0.995, gradboth l2 1.000, l1 1.000, cos 1.000, nn 0.996, hs 0.899, chroma 0.869, ab gradboth 0.973. The choice of Lab over ab, of gradboth over no gradient, and the three-way tie at 1.000 all follow from clip1 numbers. The tie-break lands on l2 because l1 has clip1 start 0.990 against 1.000 for l2 and cos, and l2 is the default. Clip2 would have chosen differently (l1 at 0.957, or K12 gradboth at 0.941), so the selection did not follow clip2. Caveats: clip1 is saturated, so the 0.996 vs 1.000 differences are one instance and clip1 cannot really rank variants. I cannot verify that the explorer never looked at the clip2 column before choosing. Treat clip2 as a one-shot report, not a clean test of the variant choice.

COMPARISON TO BASELINE (HSV torso chi2). The selected variant does not beat it, as the explorer states (beats_baseline=false). The paired bootstrap on per-instance correctness gives:
- Block overall: +0.002 (95% CI -0.025 to +0.029), a tie.
- Block clip1: +0.028 (CI +0.009 to +0.052). Clip1 is the tuning clip, so this is optimistic.
- Block clip2, the held-out report: -0.027 (CI -0.070 to +0.016).
- Block contact: -0.041 (CI -0.089 to +0.007).
- Start overall: -0.041 (CI -0.081 to -0.002).
- Start clip2: -0.071 (CI -0.141 to -0.002).
- Start contact: -0.081 (CI -0.147 to -0.033), a significant deficit.
B-vs-R on clip2 (the navy referee vs blue gi problem that motivated the study) is 0.934 block and 0.919 start, vs 0.955 and 0.984 for the baseline. So it does not fix the motivating failure. Errors are partly complementary on clip2 block (selected-only 8, baseline-only 4, both 5), but fusion was not tested.

WHAT IT ADDS: It is a cheap, low-dimensional (33-D) colour-and-brightness profile with no leakage that transfers across clips slightly better than the baseline (0.895 and 0.963 vs 0.874 and 0.930). It is perfect on clip1 and on same-frame pairs in clip1. Its A-vs-B block accuracy is marginally higher (0.969 vs 0.954). It uses darkness through Lab L, which is what separates the navy suit from the blue gi. The brightness-free versions were worse, so the gradient alone does not recover it. Its weakness is contact and the online start protocol: its bands are not anchored to body parts and the person mask contains both bodies under overlap. That mask-mixing explanation is the explorer's untested hypothesis; I did not verify it.

COST: 2.7 ms per instance cold (about 2.0 warm) for Lab conversion, erosion and band medians, vs 0.08 ms for the baseline torso histogram, so about 30x slower.

VERDICT: The explorer's report is accurate and honest and there is no leakage, but the marker should not be adopted. It is not better than the current baseline on the held-out clip, it is significantly worse on the online gallery protocol and under contact, it costs about 30x more compute, and it does not solve the navy-referee problem. It could only be revisited as a fused complement to the torso histogram, which neither the explorer nor I tested.

explore.adds_to_baseline: Nothing measurable. Texture alone is far below the colour baseline (best 0.764 block vs 0.953). Fusing it with the HSV baseline does not help. Equal-weight fusion with GLCM gave block 0.882, start 0.959. At texture weight 0.3 it gave block 0.922 (clip1 0.972, clip2 0.893), start 0.967. The colour-only control in the same Hellinger/l2 representation scores block 0.948 (clip1 0.972, clip2 0.932), start 0.967. So texture leaves clip1 unchanged, lowers clip2 and contact accuracy (0.941 to 0.880), and leaves start-protocol numbers identical to the control at weight 0.3. What texture does carry is a weak, partly colour-independent cue that picks out the referee (smooth dark suit) from the athletes: GLCM torso R recall in clip1 is 20 of 22 uncontacted. That is a darkness/smoothness effect, not weave. Post-hoc observation, not used for selection: multi-scale zoned LBP (V2) gives B-vs-R on clip2 of 0.886 block and 0.977 start, but it was not the clip1 winner and still falls short of the colour baseline overall.
explore.failure_modes: The blue-gi athlete B is the weak class. In clip1 under the block protocol (diagnostic confusion, GLCM torso), B is classed as A in 21 of 71 cases and as R in 12 of 40 uncontacted cases. In clip2, 9 of 27 contacted R instances are classed as A, because the segmenter mask in contact includes the athletes' pixels. A is classed correctly most of the time (about 90 to 98 percent). Contact accuracy is only 0.704 against the baseline's 0.954. Why it fails: (1) The clips are phone screen recordings of a YouTube stream, so the weave is not resolved. At crop resolution only coarse folds and shading survive. The native-resolution variant V15 did not fix this: clip1 0.771 (not selected), clip2 0.788, start 0.821. (2) Texture amplitude is confounded with darkness and saturation, since a blown-out white gi and a dark smooth suit are both flat. The GLCM percentile stretch partly normalises this, but a smooth blue gi region looks similar to both. (3) The person mask is a whole-frame segmenter output, so in contact the opponent's cloth leaks into the statistic. Keypoint-placed torso rectangles (V7, V9) did not fix this and were worse on clip1. (4) Rotation-invariant LBP and Gabor energy are noisy at this resolution (V1 0.539, V3 0.607, V4 0.594). Per-limb gradient energy (V6) is nearly random on clip1 (0.298) because limb keypoints are unreliable in grappling poses. (5) Nearest-neighbour prototypes (V10) overfit with only about 20 to 80 instances per class (clip1 0.610). Caveats: all 15 evaluations are listed and none were skipped, and the winner was chosen on clip1 block balanced accuracy only. glcm_torso/nn (V10) shares a feature function with the winner and counts as its own variant. The fusion weight 0.3 (V13) was a single a-priori guess, not tuned. Heterogeneous-block weights in V11, V12 and V13 were fixed a priori. Texture here uses no colour. Darkness is implicit in the percentile stretch and in log-grey contrast. The two fusion variants and the control use the HSV baseline histogram by design. glcm_torso_native reads the full-resolution video frames at feature time, using the frame index only to look up pixels. 5) IMPLEMENTATION CAVEAT, not disclosed by the explorer. The checkpoint's 5 non-local blocks (65 tensors) are silently dropped by strict=False, and the input is 256x128 where the config uses 384x128. I built a faithful SBS-R50 as a diagnostic, in scratch only. explore.notes: Family: context_motion (non-appearance). Code is only in tools/markers/context_motion.py (no other repo file changed). It exports FEATURES, META, DIAGNOSTIC and BEST, and `PYTHONPATH=. python tools/markers/context_motion.py [names]` runs the harness. Features use only the raw detections (box, conf, keypoints) of the instance's clip, linked frame to frame by mutual-best IoU >= 0.3 with a height ratio <= 1.5 (so cuts break links). Each variant uses window W of 2, 4 or 8 frames on each side. Quantities: log speed of the box centre (/box height), articulation (mean displacement of keypoints relative to the box centre, /box height; invariant to a camera pan), log |dh| and |d aspect| rates, log aspect, height relative to the median of the other confident persons in the frame, height / frame height (608), nearest-person distance and IoU, and net/path displacement. All lengths are divided by the person's own box height. Velocity direction, absolute position, frame index, crop size and time are never used. No colour or darkness, no training, and prototype scaling is hard-coded (log floor 0.005). Protocol: 14 variants were declared in code and run, all listed (limit 15). Selection used clip1 block balanced accuracy among non-diagnostic variants only: artic_only_W4 0.634, motion_shape_W4 0.633, speed_artic_W2 0.625. The harness prints clip2 for every run, so clip2 numbers were visible, but no variant, hyperparameter (W, metric, mode) or fusion was chosen by them. Two variants (rel_ctx_W4, still_narrow_W4) were added after seeing the first 12 clip1 results; I motivated them from clip1 statistics only (R: articulation 0.008 vs 0.09 for athletes; log aspect -1.1 vs about 0). Timing for the best variant is 0.87 ms/instance cold, including the raw-detection npz load, and 0.74 ms with chains recomputed. Clip1 per-class means for A/B/R (instances A 78, B 71, R 22) gave R speed 0.007 vs 0.04-0.07 box-heights/frame. Bottom line: this family does not beat the colour baseline (0.57 vs 0.953 block) and cannot identify a unique athlete. The only value is as a stationarity/upright veto for the referee, which fixes the baseline's four navy-suit errors in clip2, and it needs a calibrated gate before it can be fused.

No segment, clip or position leakage found. Code read: artic_only_W4 uses only lart, ldh and lda. These are mean keypoint displacement relative to the box centre divided by box height, plus the absolute log change in box height and in aspect between IoU-linked neighbouring frames. No pixels, crop width, mask area, frame index, absolute position or colour/darkness are features. inst['clip'] and inst['frame'] are used only to look up neighbouring raw detections.

Tests run:
(1) Transforming all raw detections of each clip by a random uniform scale and translation (0.43x/+713,-251 for clip1; 2.7x/-400,+90 for clip2) changed the features by at most 5.6e-5, with identical abstentions. The feature is position and scale invariant.
(2) 300 label shuffles per scheme, within clip, within 24-frame block and within frame, collapsed 3-class block balanced accuracy to 0.33-0.35 (sd 0.04-0.06; 95th percentile 0.41-0.45). The real 0.634 (clip1) and 0.517 (clip2) are both above the 95th percentile (p<0.003 on 300 permutations), so the signal is real and the pipeline has no label or time channel.
(3) A control feature built from the median lart, ldh and lda of all people in the frame (identical for every person in a frame) gave 3-class block 0.397 on clip1 and 0.333 on clip2. That is chance within noise, so no time-phase composition leak.
(4) The R-vs-{A,B} signal is not just the overlap-based labelling rule. Against non-contact athletes only, AUC(R less articulated) is 0.878 on clip1 and 0.846 on clip2 (0.935 for contact athletes on clip2). Binary R-vs-athletes block balanced accuracy on the non-contact subset is 0.771 (clip1) and 0.678 (clip2).

(a) Articulation correlates with box height among athletes (r about -0.65 to -0.80) because it tracks posture/phase (standing vs ground work). It does not correlate within R (r about 0.04).
